claim: Bone surfaces were scarcely occupied by small and flat osteoblasts in mice bearing a germline deletion of Tgif1 compared to control littermates.
source: Further histological examination revealed that bone surfaces were scarcely occupied by small and flat osteoblasts in mice bearing a germline deletion of Tgif1 (Figure 1A, Figure 1—source data 1) or a deletion of Tgif1 targeted to osteoblasts (Figure 1B) compared to control littermates.
evidence: Supported by histological images in Figure 1A and 1B showing toluidine blue staining of bone sections from Tgif1-deficient and control mice.

claim: Tgif1-deficient osteoblasts might be compromised in acquiring a physiological osteoblast morphology.
source: This finding suggested that Tgif1-deficient osteoblasts might, in addition to an impaired bone matrix-producing capacity (Saito et al., 2019) be compromised in acquiring a physiological osteoblast morphology.
evidence: Based on inference from histological observations and cited prior work on impaired bone matrix production.

claim: Calvarial osteoblasts from Tgif1-deficient mice were impaired in their ability to attach to collagen type I-coated surfaces throughout a 4 hr time-course.
source: In support of our hypothesis that Tgif1-deficiency compromises morphological plasticity of osteoblasts, calvarial- and long bone-derived osteoblasts obtained from Tgif1-deficient mice were impaired in their ability to attach to collagen type I-coated surfaces throughout a 4 hr time-course (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: Quantitative data shown in Figure 1D and 1E demonstrating reduced adherence at 1, 2, and 4 hours.

claim: Long bone-derived osteoblasts obtained from Tgif1-deficient mice were impaired in their ability to attach to collagen type I-coated surfaces throughout a 4 hr time-course.
source: In support of our hypothesis that Tgif1-deficiency compromises morphological plasticity of osteoblasts, calvarial- and long bone-derived osteoblasts obtained from Tgif1-deficient mice were impaired in their ability to attach to collagen type I-coated surfaces throughout a 4 hr time-course (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: Quantitative data shown in Figure 1E demonstrating reduced adherence at 1, 2, and 4 hours.

claim: Osteoblasts lacking Tgif1 were impaired in their migration capacity reflected by a shorter track length.
source: This analysis revealed that osteoblasts lacking Tgif1 were impaired in their migration capacity reflected by a shorter track length, a reduced velocity, and a less straight and, therefore, more meandering track path (Figure 1F–H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Live cell video microscopy data quantified in Figure 1F showing reduced track length.

claim: Osteoblasts lacking Tgif1 were impaired in their migration capacity reflected by a reduced velocity.
source: This analysis revealed that osteoblasts lacking Tgif1 were impaired in their migration capacity reflected by a shorter track length, a reduced velocity, and a less straight and, therefore, more meandering track path (Figure 1F–H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Live cell video microscopy data quantified in Figure 1G showing reduced velocity.

claim: Osteoblasts lacking Tgif1 were impaired in their migration capacity reflected by a more meandering track path.
source: This analysis revealed that osteoblasts lacking Tgif1 were impaired in their migration capacity reflected by a shorter track length, a reduced velocity, and a less straight and, therefore, more meandering track path (Figure 1F–H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Live cell video microscopy data quantified in Figure 1H showing increased meandering index.

claim: Tgif1 is important for osteoblasts to adhere and migrate on collagen type I-rich surfaces.
source: Thus, these in vivo and in vitro data indicate that Tgif1 is important for osteoblasts to adhere and migrate on collagen type I-rich surfaces.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple in vitro adhesion and migration assays presented in Figure 1.

claim: Osteoblasts lacking Tgif1 adhered less to collagen type I matrix and were impaired in their capacities to migrate into the matrix compared to control cells.
source: In support of the previous observations, osteoblasts lacking Tgif1 adhered less to collagen type I matrix and were impaired in their capacities to migrate into the matrix compared to control cells (Figure 1J).
evidence: 3D cell culture experiment shown in Figure 1J with H&E staining.

claim: Tgif1-deficient osteoblasts were rather flat in morphology and smaller in size as determined by reduced cell area and perimeter.
source: The experiment also confirmed that Tgif1-deficient osteoblasts were rather flat in morphology and smaller in size as determined by reduced cell area and perimeter (Figure 1K–M).
evidence: Quantitative morphometric analysis shown in Figure 1L and 1M from phalloidin-stained sections.

claim: Tgif1 is indispensable for osteoblasts to adapt a regular cell morphology and to adhere and migrate on collagen type I-rich matrices in vitro and on bone surfaces in vivo.
source: Collectively, these observations demonstrate that Tgif1 is indispensable for osteoblasts to adapt a regular cell morphology and to adhere and migrate on collagen type I-rich matrices in vitro and on bone surfaces in vivo.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on multiple in vitro and in vivo experiments presented in Figure 1.

claim: Tgif1-/- osteoblasts were significantly impaired in their ability to spread during a 60 minute experiment compared to control cells.
source: Compared to control cells, Tgif1-/- osteoblasts were significantly impaired in their ability to spread during the experiment (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Calcein-AM live cell spreading assay quantified in Figure 2B showing increased percentage of non-spread cells.

claim: After 60 min of culture on collagen type I-coated surfaces, Tgif1-deficient osteoblasts were less spread and had a greater sphericity.
source: Consistently, after 60 min of culture on collagen type I-coated surfaces, Tgif1-deficient osteoblasts were less spread and, therefore, had a greater sphericity (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: 3D reconstruction and sphericity analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Tgif1-deficient osteoblasts that underwent spreading formed less cellular processes and focal adhesions compared to control cells.
source: Furthermore, Tgif1-deficient osteoblasts that underwent spreading formed less cellular processes and focal adhesions compared to control cells (Figure 2C and E).
evidence: Immunofluorescence imaging and quantification of focal adhesions shown in Figure 2C and 2E.

claim: siRNA-mediated silencing of Tgif1 in OCY454 cells resulted in an impaired cell spreading with a consecutive higher cell sphericity.
source: Consistent with the findings made by genetic deletion of Tgif1, siRNA-mediated silencing of Tgif1 in OCY454 cells resulted in an impaired cell spreading with a consecutive higher cell sphericity and a decrease in focal adhesion formation (Figure 2F–H).
evidence: siRNA knockdown experiment with sphericity quantification shown in Figure 2G.

claim: siRNA-mediated silencing of Tgif1 in OCY454 cells resulted in a decrease in focal adhesion formation.
source: Consistent with the findings made by genetic deletion of Tgif1, siRNA-mediated silencing of Tgif1 in OCY454 cells resulted in an impaired cell spreading with a consecutive higher cell sphericity and a decrease in focal adhesion formation (Figure 2F–H).
evidence: siRNA knockdown experiment with focal adhesion quantification shown in Figure 2H.

claim: No major changes were identified in the expression or activation of FAK, Integrin β1, Src, talin, paxillin, p38, and LRG5 in the absence of Tgif1 during cell spreading.
source: However, no major changes were identified in the expression or activation of these molecules in the absence of Tgif1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: Western blot analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Tgif1 is predominantly localized in the nucleus and to some extent in the cytoplasm.
source: Immunocytochemistry revealed that Tgif1 is predominantly localized in the nucleus and to some extend in the cytoplasm (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Immunocytochemistry images shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Cytoplasmic Tgif1 did not interact with focal adhesions, because no co-localization of eGFP-Tgif1 with paxillin or talin was observed.
source: However, cytoplasmic Tgif1 did not interact with focal adhesions, because no co-localization of eGFP-Tgif1 neither with paxillin nor with talin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) was observed.
evidence: Co-localization immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Expression of Cdc42es2, Cdc42ep1, Cdc42ep2, or Cdc42ep4 was not changed in the absence of Tgif1 during osteoblast adhesion and spreading.
source: However, expression of none of the Cdc42 family members Cdc42es2, Cdc42ep1, Cdc42ep2, or Cdc42ep4 was changed in the absence of Tgif1 during osteoblast adhesion and spreading (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2—source data 1).
evidence: qPCR gene expression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-D.

claim: Expression of Pak1, Pak2, and Pak4 was unchanged in Tgif1-deficient osteoblasts during adhesion and spreading.
source: While expression of Pak1, Pak2, and Pak4 was unchanged in Tgif1-deficient osteoblasts during adhesion and spreading (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E–G), expression of Pak3 was strongly increased in Tgif1-deficient osteoblasts compared to control cells at the mRNA and protein level prior to and 60 min after adhesion (Figure 3A and B, Figure 3—source data 1–3).
evidence: qPCR gene expression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E-G.

claim: Expression of Pak3 was strongly increased in Tgif1-deficient osteoblasts compared to control cells at the mRNA and protein level prior to and 60 min after adhesion.
source: While expression of Pak1, Pak2, and Pak4 was unchanged in Tgif1-deficient osteoblasts during adhesion and spreading (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E–G), expression of Pak3 was strongly increased in Tgif1-deficient osteoblasts compared to control cells at the mRNA and protein level prior to and 60 min after adhesion (Figure 3A and B, Figure 3—source data 1–3).
evidence: qPCR and Western blot data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: Expression of Pak3 mRNA showed a trend towards an increase in bones from Tgif1-/- mice compared to control littermates.
source: Confirming this observation in vivo, expression of Pak3 mRNA showed a trend towards an increase in bones from Tgif1-/- mice compared to control littermates (Figure 3C).
evidence: qPCR analysis of tibiae shown in Figure 3C with p=0.07.

claim: Tgif1 bound to the predicted promoter binding site of Pak3.
source: Indeed, Tgif1 bound to the predicted promoter binding site and to a site of the Rar promoter as positive control (Zhang et al., 2009), but not to a DNA sequence lacking predicted Tgif1 binding site as negative control (Figure 3D), suggesting a regulation of the Pak3 promoter activity by Tgif1.
evidence: Chromatin immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Silencing of Tgif1 led to a significant increase in luciferase activity of the Pak3 promoter compared to control.
source: Silencing of Tgif1 lead to a significant increase in luciferase activity compared to control (Figure 3E) demonstrating that Tgif1 is a transcriptional repressor of the Pak3 promoter.
evidence: Luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Tgif1 is a transcriptional repressor of the Pak3 promoter.
source: Silencing of Tgif1 lead to a significant increase in luciferase activity compared to control (Figure 3E) demonstrating that Tgif1 is a transcriptional repressor of the Pak3 promoter.
evidence: Conclusion based on luciferase reporter assay showing increased promoter activity upon Tgif1 silencing.

claim: Attenuating Pak3 expression restored the Tgif1 deficiency-mediated impaired cell spreading.
source: Indeed, attenuating Pak3 expression restored the Tgif1 deficiency-mediated impaired cell spreading (Figure 3F).
evidence: siRNA rescue experiment shown in Figure 3F with immunofluorescence imaging.

claim: Pak3 silencing reduced the Tgif1 deficiency-dependent gain in cell sphericity.
source: Since cells are less spherical upon spreading, Pak3 silencing reduced the Tgif1 deficiency-dependent gain in cell sphericity and restored the number of focal adhesions per cell that were reduced by Tgif1 deficiency to the level of control (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: Sphericity quantification shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Pak3 silencing restored the number of focal adhesions per cell that were reduced by Tgif1 deficiency to the level of control.
source: Since cells are less spherical upon spreading, Pak3 silencing reduced the Tgif1 deficiency-dependent gain in cell sphericity and restored the number of focal adhesions per cell that were reduced by Tgif1 deficiency to the level of control (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: Focal adhesion quantification shown in Figure 3H.

claim: In the absence of Tgif1, the Pak3 promoter is de-repressed, leading to an increased transcriptional activity and Pak3 expression.
source: Together, these findings demonstrate that in the absence of Tgif1, the Pak3 promoter is de-repressed, leading to an increased transcriptional activity and Pak3 expression.
evidence: Conclusion based on ChIP, luciferase, and expression data from Figure 3.

claim: A higher abundance of Pak3 suppresses focal adhesion formation and osteoblast spreading.
source: A higher abundance of Pak3 in turn suppresses focal adhesion formation and osteoblast spreading.
evidence: Conclusion based on rescue experiments showing restoration of spreading and focal adhesions upon Pak3 silencing.

claim: Tgif1 mRNA expression was significantly increased within 20 min of spreading with a further increase after 60 min in calvarial osteoblasts.
source: Both, Tgif1 mRNA and protein expression were significantly increased within 20 min of spreading with a further increase after 60 min in calvarial osteoblasts (Figure 4A and B, Figure 4—source data 1) and in OCY454 cells (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: qPCR and Western blot data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: Tgif1 protein expression was significantly increased within 20 min of spreading with a further increase after 60 min in calvarial osteoblasts.
source: Both, Tgif1 mRNA and protein expression were significantly increased within 20 min of spreading with a further increase after 60 min in calvarial osteoblasts (Figure 4A and B, Figure 4—source data 1) and in OCY454 cells (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Tgif1 mRNA and protein expression were significantly increased within 20 min of spreading with a further increase after 60 min in OCY454 cells.
source: Both, Tgif1 mRNA and protein expression were significantly increased within 20 min of spreading with a further increase after 60 min in calvarial osteoblasts (Figure 4A and B, Figure 4—source data 1) and in OCY454 cells (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: qPCR and Western blot data shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: Treatment with Actinomycin-D fully prevented the increase in Tgif1 mRNA expression during osteoblast spreading.
source: To determine if the increase in Tgif1 abundance is transcriptionally regulated, osteoblasts were treated with the transcription inhibitor Actinomycin-D during spreading, which fully prevented the increase in Tgif1 mRNA expression (Figure 4E).
evidence: qPCR data with Actinomycin-D treatment shown in Figure 4E.

claim: ERK1/2 inhibition prevented the increase of Tgif1 mRNA expression during the first 20 min of osteoblast spreading.
source: Although ERK1/2 inhibition prevented the increase of Tgif1 mRNA expression during the first 20 min of osteoblast spreading, it failed to suppress Tgif1 mRNA expression 60 min after initiation of osteoblast spreading (Figure 4G).
evidence: qPCR data with ERK1/2 inhibitor treatment shown in Figure 4G.

claim: ERK1/2 inhibition failed to suppress Tgif1 mRNA expression 60 min after initiation of osteoblast spreading.
source: Although ERK1/2 inhibition prevented the increase of Tgif1 mRNA expression during the first 20 min of osteoblast spreading, it failed to suppress Tgif1 mRNA expression 60 min after initiation of osteoblast spreading (Figure 4G).
evidence: qPCR data with ERK1/2 inhibitor treatment shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The increase in Tgif1 mRNA expression at early stages of osteoblast spreading is mediated by ERK1/2 signaling.
source: This finding suggests that the increase in Tgif1 mRNA expression at early stages of osteoblast spreading is mediated by ERK1/2 signaling while it is independent of ERK1/2 signaling at later stages of osteoblast spreading.
evidence: Conclusion based on ERK1/2 inhibitor experiments showing time-dependent effects.

claim: The increase in Tgif1 mRNA expression at later stages of osteoblast spreading is independent of ERK1/2 signaling.
source: This finding suggests that the increase in Tgif1 mRNA expression at early stages of osteoblast spreading is mediated by ERK1/2 signaling while it is independent of ERK1/2 signaling at later stages of osteoblast spreading.
evidence: Conclusion based on ERK1/2 inhibitor experiments showing no effect at 60 min.

claim: The 2.2 kb and 1.7 kb fragments of the human TGIF1 promoter were fully activated after 60 min of osteoblast spreading.
source: While the 2.2 kb and 1.7 kb fragments of the human TGIF1 promoter were fully activated after 60 min of osteoblast spreading, no activation of the 1.2 kb and 0.5 kb fragments was observed (Figure 4H), suggesting that the regulatory promoter region that is activated during osteoblast spreading must be located within the 500 bp between the 1.7 kb and the 1.2 kb promoter fragments.
evidence: Luciferase reporter assay with promoter truncations shown in Figure 4H.

claim: No activation of the 1.2 kb and 0.5 kb fragments of the human TGIF1 promoter was observed after 60 min of osteoblast spreading.
source: While the 2.2 kb and 1.7 kb fragments of the human TGIF1 promoter were fully activated after 60 min of osteoblast spreading, no activation of the 1.2 kb and 0.5 kb fragments was observed (Figure 4H), suggesting that the regulatory promoter region that is activated during osteoblast spreading must be located within the 500 bp between the 1.7 kb and the 1.2 kb promoter fragments.
evidence: Luciferase reporter assay with promoter truncations shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The regulatory promoter region that is activated during osteoblast spreading must be located within the 500 bp between the 1.7 kb and the 1.2 kb promoter fragments.
source: While the 2.2 kb and 1.7 kb fragments of the human TGIF1 promoter were fully activated after 60 min of osteoblast spreading, no activation of the 1.2 kb and 0.5 kb fragments was observed (Figure 4H), suggesting that the regulatory promoter region that is activated during osteoblast spreading must be located within the 500 bp between the 1.7 kb and the 1.2 kb promoter fragments.
evidence: Inference from promoter truncation analysis showing differential activation patterns.

claim: AP1-signaling is activated 60 min after initiation of osteoblast spreading.
source: The findings demonstrate that AP1-signaling is activated 60 min after initiation of osteoblast spreading (Figure 4I), indicating a potential implication of AP1 signaling during advanced stages of osteoblast spreading.
evidence: AP1 luciferase reporter assay shown in Figure 4I.

claim: The wild-type TGIF1 promoter was fully activated after 60 min of osteoblast spreading.
source: Although the wild-type promoter was fully activated after 60 min of osteoblast spreading, the TGIF1 promoter bearing the disabled AP1 binding site was not activated (Figure 4J).
evidence: Luciferase reporter assay comparing wild-type and AP1 mutant promoters shown in Figure 4J.

claim: The TGIF1 promoter bearing the disabled AP1 binding site was not activated after 60 min of osteoblast spreading.
source: Although the wild-type promoter was fully activated after 60 min of osteoblast spreading, the TGIF1 promoter bearing the disabled AP1 binding site was not activated (Figure 4J).
evidence: Luciferase reporter assay comparing wild-type and AP1 mutant promoters shown in Figure 4J.

claim: AP1 signaling is involved in the activation of Tgif1 gene expression during later stages of osteoblast spreading.
source: These findings suggest that AP1 signaling is involved in the activation of Tgif1 gene expression during later stages of osteoblast spreading.
evidence: Conclusion based on AP1 reporter assays and AP1 binding site mutation experiments.

claim: In mice bearing a germline deletion of Tgif1, the callus was less ossified and the trabeculae in the repair zone were sparsely occupied by fewer, thinner, and less-active osteoblasts compared to control mice.
source: In contrast, in mice bearing a germline deletion of Tgif1, the callus was less ossified and the trabeculae in the repair zone were sparsely occupied by fewer, thinner, and less-active osteoblasts (Figure 5A–F).
evidence: Histological and µCT analysis of fracture healing shown in Figure 5A-F.

claim: Tgif1 is important for bone regeneration.
source: These findings demonstrate that Tgif1 is important for bone regeneration.
evidence: Conclusion based on fracture healing experiments showing impaired bone repair in Tgif1-deficient mice.

claim: PTH treatment greatly increased the number of active osteoblasts and induces the acquisition of a cuboidal shape and the percentage of active bone surfaces.
source: Consistent with the findings reported by others and in support of our hypothesis, PTH treatment greatly increased the number of active osteoblasts and induces the acquisition of a cuboidal shape and consequently the percentage of active bone surfaces (Kousteni and Bilezikian, 2008; Tam et al., 1982), which all occurred at a much lesser extent in mice lacking Tgif1 (Figure 6A and B, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Histomorphometric analysis shown in Figure 6A and 6B with citations to prior work.

claim: PTH-induced osteoblast recruitment, adaptation of a cuboidal morphology, and activation of bone surfaces occurred at a much lesser extent in mice lacking Tgif1.
source: Consistent with the findings reported by others and in support of our hypothesis, PTH treatment greatly increased the number of active osteoblasts and induces the acquisition of a cuboidal shape and consequently the percentage of active bone surfaces (Kousteni and Bilezikian, 2008; Tam et al., 1982), which all occurred at a much lesser extent in mice lacking Tgif1 (Figure 6A and B, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Histomorphometric analysis shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: PTH treatment induced osteoblast recruitment, adaptation of a cuboidal morphology of matrix-producing osteoblasts, and a profound activation of bone surfaces by osteoblasts in control animals, but these effects were much less pronounced in mice lacking Tgif1 in osteoblasts.
source: Indeed, while PTH treatment induced osteoblast recruitment, adaptation of a cuboidal morphology of matrix-producing osteoblasts, and a profound activation of bone surfaces by osteoblasts in control animals, these effects were much less pronounced in mice lacking Tgif1 in osteoblasts (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: Histomorphometric analysis of osteoblast-specific Tgif1 deletion shown in Figure 6C and 6D.

claim: PTH-dependent bone surface activation is attenuated in the absence of Tgif1 in osteoblasts.
source: These findings, therefore, demonstrate that PTH-dependent bone surface activation is attenuated in the absence of Tgif1 in osteoblasts.
evidence: Conclusion based on PTH treatment experiments in Tgif1-deficient mice showing reduced bone surface activation.

claim: PTH supports osteoblast spreading.
source: Immunofluorescence staining and quantification of cell sphericity revealed that PTH supports osteoblast spreading (Figure 7A and B, Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: Immunofluorescence and sphericity analysis shown in Figure 7A and 7B.

claim: PTH treatment of cells in which Tgif1 expression was silenced failed to induce the spreading of osteoblasts.
source: Furthermore, PTH treatment of cells in which Tgif1 expression was silenced failed to induce the spreading of osteoblasts (Figure 7A and B), demonstrating that the PTH-mediated osteoblast spreading indeed depends on Tgif1.
evidence: siRNA knockdown with PTH treatment shown in Figure 7A and 7B.

claim: PTH-mediated osteoblast spreading depends on Tgif1.
source: Furthermore, PTH treatment of cells in which Tgif1 expression was silenced failed to induce the spreading of osteoblasts (Figure 7A and B), demonstrating that the PTH-mediated osteoblast spreading indeed depends on Tgif1.
evidence: Conclusion based on rescue experiments showing PTH fails to induce spreading when Tgif1 is silenced.

claim: Pak3 mRNA expression was reduced upon PTH treatment.
source: Indeed, Pak3 mRNA expression was reduced upon PTH treatment (Figure 7C).
evidence: qPCR data showing Pak3 expression after PTH treatment shown in Figure 7C.

claim: PTH treatment increased Tgif1 expression and reduced PAK3 protein abundance in control cells but not in osteoblasts in which Tgif1 expression was silenced by siRNA.
source: In addition, PTH treatment increased Tgif1 expression and reduced PAK3 protein abundance in control cells but not in osteoblasts in which Tgif1 expression was silenced by siRNA (Figure 7D, Figure 7—source data 2 and 3).
evidence: Western blot analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Silencing Tgif1 expression impaired osteoblast spreading induced by PTH treatment, which was restored by the concomitant silencing of Pak3 expression.
source: Immunofluorescence staining and quantification of cell sphericity revealed that silencing Tgif1 expression impaired osteoblast spreading induced by PTH treatment, which was restored by the concomitant silencing of Pak3 expression (Figure 7E and F).
evidence: Double knockdown rescue experiment shown in Figure 7E and 7F.

claim: Lack of both Tgif1 and PAK3 prevented PTH-induced decrease in cell sphericity.
source: Furthermore, lack of both, Tgif1 and PAK3 prevented PTH-induced decrease in cell sphericity.
evidence: Conclusion based on sphericity measurements in double knockdown experiments with PTH treatment.

claim: An increased abundance of PAK3 in response to Tgif1-deficiency impairs PTH-induced spreading of osteoblasts.
source: These findings indicate that an increased abundance of PAK3 in response to Tgif1-deficiency impairs PTH-induced spreading of osteoblasts and that PTH facilitates osteoblast spreading via Tgif1-PAK3 signaling.
evidence: Conclusion based on rescue experiments showing PAK3 knockdown restores PTH-induced spreading in Tgif1-deficient cells.

claim: PTH facilitates osteoblast spreading via Tgif1-PAK3 signaling.
source: These findings indicate that an increased abundance of PAK3 in response to Tgif1-deficiency impairs PTH-induced spreading of osteoblasts and that PTH facilitates osteoblast spreading via Tgif1-PAK3 signaling.
evidence: Conclusion based on multiple experiments showing PTH effects on spreading depend on Tgif1-PAK3 axis.

claim: Tgif1 suppresses Pak3 expression in osteoblasts via the ERK1/2 and AP1 signaling pathways.
source: In summary, our results reveal that Tgif1 suppresses Pak3 expression in osteoblasts via the ERK1/2 and AP1 signaling pathways, which is important for osteoblasts to form focal adhesions, to spread on bone surfaces, and to migrate.
evidence: Summary conclusion integrating multiple experimental findings from the study.

claim: Tgif1 is important for osteoblasts to form focal adhesions, to spread on bone surfaces, and to migrate.
source: In summary, our results reveal that Tgif1 suppresses Pak3 expression in osteoblasts via the ERK1/2 and AP1 signaling pathways, which is important for osteoblasts to form focal adhesions, to spread on bone surfaces, and to migrate.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on multiple functional assays throughout the study.

claim: The Tgif1-PAK3 mechanism is implicated in bone regeneration and in the pharmacological effects of PTH treatment.
source: This mechanism is implicated in bone regeneration and in the pharmacological effects of PTH treatment and is, therefore, of translational relevance.
evidence: Conclusion based on in vivo fracture healing and PTH treatment experiments.

claim: Bone remodeling is a highly coordinated and continuously ongoing process involving osteoblasts, osteoclasts, and osteocytes.
source: Bone remodeling is a highly coordinated and continuously ongoing process involving osteoblasts, osteoclasts, and osteocytes, that interact with each other and function in concert to maintain bone mass and preserve the integrity of the skeletal system (Baron and Hesse, 2012).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Baron and Hesse, 2012.

claim: Osteoblasts are derived from mesenchymal stem cells.
source: Osteoblasts, derived from mesenchymal stem cells, play a pivotal role in synthesizing and depositing collagen type I-rich bone matrix (Ponzetti and Rucci, 2021).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Ponzetti and Rucci, 2021.

claim: Osteoblasts play a pivotal role in synthesizing and depositing collagen type I-rich bone matrix.
source: Osteoblasts, derived from mesenchymal stem cells, play a pivotal role in synthesizing and depositing collagen type I-rich bone matrix (Ponzetti and Rucci, 2021).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Ponzetti and Rucci, 2021.

claim: Multiple factors influence osteoblast migration, including growth factors, cytokines, signaling pathways like bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs) and transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β) as well as interactions with other cells and the extracellular matrix.
source: Multiple factors influence osteoblast migration, including growth factors, cytokines, signaling pathways like bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs) and transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β) as well as interactions with other cells and the extracellular matrix (Thiel et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Thiel et al., 2018.

claim: Teriparatide is a recombinant form of the first 34 amino acids of human parathyroid hormone.
source: Teriparatide, a recombinant form of the first 34 amino acids of human parathyroid hormone (rhPTH1-34; hereafter PTH), is a bone anabolic drug used to treat severe osteoporosis, characterized by low bone mineral density and an increased fracture risk (Neer et al., 2001; Black and Rosen, 2016).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to Neer et al., 2001 and Black and Rosen, 2016.

claim: PTH treatment stimulates bone formation by increasing the number, differentiation, and activity of osteoblasts.
source: PTH treatment stimulates bone formation by increasing the number, differentiation, and activity of osteoblasts (Pettway et al., 2008; Silva et al., 2011; Ogita et al., 2008).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to Pettway et al., 2008; Silva et al., 2011; Ogita et al., 2008.

claim: Tgif1 was identified as PTH target gene.
source: Furthermore, Tgif1 was identified as PTH target gene, and in the absence of Tgif1, PTH treatment failed to increase bone mass in mice (Saito et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Saito et al., 2019.

claim: In the absence of Tgif1, PTH treatment failed to increase bone mass in mice.
source: Furthermore, Tgif1 was identified as PTH target gene, and in the absence of Tgif1, PTH treatment failed to increase bone mass in mice (Saito et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Saito et al., 2019.
